prize_parts.citation: For showing how technology, task content and trade exposure reshape labour demand, wage inequality and local labour-market adjustment.

statement.case_for: The contribution joins a conceptual account of labour demand (skill-biased change, then tasks and polarisation) with credible quasi-experimental evidence on what import competition does to local labour markets. It changed which questions economists ask about technology and trade, and how they measure adjustment costs. It also changed how the distributional consequences of both are discussed in research and policy. The results have been replicated, extended and challenged for more than a decade, so the core findings have been tested, which matters for maturity. What the evidence identifies is also unusually clear: the China-shock designs identify local employment, earnings and migration responses to exposure. That is a well-defined causal object even where the aggregate welfare implications are not identified. My opening ranking is unchanged after reading colleagues' arguments. B036 has the thinnest support among my top choices, and I have tried to test it against the criticisms rather than rely on that ranking.
statement.case_against: The candidate bundles two strands with partly different authorship and different vintages: the skill-premium and task framework, and the China-shock evidence. A three-name set therefore under-credits someone whichever way it is drawn. Dorn is a core co-author of the trade-shock papers, and the task-model lineage extends to contributors who are not credited here, notably Acemoglu and Restrepo. The size, persistence and external validity of the trade-shock estimates remain contested. Much of the evidence is reduced-form and identifies local effects rather than aggregate welfare effects. If the committee wants a single clean discovery with unambiguous credit, other shortlisted candidates may fit that standard better.

responses.point: Friberg proposes Autor, Dorn and Hanson, treating the China shock as the core of the case. He regards its maturity as moderate to high and notes that the identification and external validity of the shift-share design have been debated. He also notes that the tasks-and-technology literature has other contributors, so the boundary of the discovery is unclear.
responses.response: I accept the identification point, but I think the debate over exposure designs and shift-share inference has refined the estimates more than it has overturned the qualitative findings on local adjustment costs. I also think his proposal shows why the boundary question matters. If the citation is narrowly the China shock, Dorn belongs in the set and Katz does not. If the citation is the broader account of technology, tasks, trade and wage structure, Katz's skill-premium and polarisation work is part of the discovery and Dorn, the most junior of the China-shock authors, is the one left out. I prefer the broader framing because it is the larger conceptual contribution, but Dorn in place of Katz is a defensible alternative that I would not oppose on scientific grounds.

responses.point: Hassler ranks the New Keynesian framework (B015) first. He cites its durable influence on monetary-policy analysis and practice, and he says the main difficulty is choosing three laureates from a crowded field, with Woodford, Taylor and Calvo as his trio.
responses.response: I agree that B015 has the larger footprint on policy practice, which is why I list it as my first alternative. My hesitation is attribution, not merit, and Hassler's own uncertainties acknowledge the same difficulty. Several colleagues, Hassler among them, converge on Woodford, Taylor and Calvo, which I find a more defensible way to credit the building blocks than my own Woodford, Galí, Taylor selection. If B015 were the vehicle, I would move toward that trio. I still weigh two things against it. The post-2021 inflation episode and the heterogeneous-agent critique leave the framework's empirical standing more open than the label 'fully mature' suggests. Credit for estimation and quantification (Galí, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets) is also excluded under a three-name cap. B036 has a more tightly bounded credit set, and I think that offsets its smaller policy footprint.

responses.point: Stromberg ranks B036 third and calls the evidence high-quality across trade, labour and technology. He flags the debate over the magnitude and persistence of the China-shock effects, and he lists overlap with the 2024 prize to Acemoglu as an uncertainty.
responses.response: I share the concern about magnitude and persistence and have listed it among my own reservations. On the overlap, I would qualify the framing. As I understand it, the 2024 recognition concerned how institutions are formed and affect prosperity, not task-based models of technology and labour demand, so any overlap lies in the task-model lineage rather than in the prize's cited subject. That is still a real attribution issue, because it is the reason Acemoglu and Restrepo's task work sits outside this credited set. I read it as an argument for defining the citation around the empirical task-and-trade findings of Autor, Hanson and Katz. I do not read it as an argument against the candidate. Stromberg ranks B050 first, and I would like him to say whether the collateral-constraint case, with Gertler and Gilchrist excluded, clears the bar on attribution that he applies to B036.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats the skill-premium and task framework and the China-shock evidence as one discovery or two, which determines whether Katz or Dorn is the right third name.
How far the China-shock estimates of local effects generalise across countries and periods, and how much their persistence depends on design choices.
How much credit for task-based models belongs to contributors outside the credited names, and whether that undercuts a three-name prize.
Whether B015's wider policy reach should outweigh its diffuse attribution, and which trio would best represent it.
My assessments rest on general knowledge and the supplied materials, not on independent verification of the scientific record.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. The profile shows no co-authorship or institutional tie to Autor, Hanson, Katz or Dorn. My field of empirical labour economics is adjacent to this candidate, so I flag that as a possible bias in how I weigh it. I have tried to apply the same criteria as for other fields.
